claims.text: The starting material is a crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticle composed of five or more metals.
Using multicomponent HEA nanoparticles is a single intervention distinct from the starting material.
Using HEA nanoparticles can overcome instability during operation at 773–1173 K.
Multicomponent HEA nanoparticles possess improved stability.
Multicomponent HEA nanoparticles have functional applications in catalysis.
Multicomponent HEA nanoparticles have functional applications in data memory.
Multicomponent HEA nanoparticles have functional applications in energy storage.
The intervention will improve nanoparticle stability relative to untreated nanoparticles in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime.
The intervention will improve nanoparticle performance relative to untreated nanoparticles in the 773–1173 K catalytic regime.
The compositional boundary requires five or more metals.
The proposed intervention is applicable to catalysis, data memory, and energy storage.
The exact mechanism by which HEA nanoparticles improve stability and performance is not fully understood.
A comparison of untreated and HEA nanoparticles under 773–1173 K catalytic operation could test the hypothesis.
No significant difference in stability and performance between untreated and HEA nanoparticles would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The starting nanoparticles are already five-or-more-component, near-equiatomic solid solutions—the defining description of HEA nanoparticles—yet the proposed intervention is simply to use HEA nanoparticles and the baseline is described as untreated nanoparticles. No actual change distinguishing intervention from baseline is specified.

Improved stability is presented simultaneously as the structural mediator, the mechanism, and the predicted outcome, making the causal account circular rather than identifying an intermediate structural change.
